## The new Interpretation Centre: an open door to the wetland

The building stands on an elevated platform that allows visitors to contemplate the water surface without interfering with the life teeming among the reeds. It is three hundred square metres conceived with a clear logic: that visitors understand, before setting foot on the trails, what they are seeing and why it deserves protection. The mayor of Motril, Luisa García Chamorro, inaugurated the space on 6 February at an event attended by municipal technicians, representatives of environmental groups and local residents. The opening of the centre marks the culmination of an adaptation process that has lasted several years and has been financed with European funds managed by the town council.

The exhibition route begins with a large-scale model that reproduces the entire wetland in miniature, from the main entrance to the most distant lagoons. On it, points of light indicate the different vegetation zones and bird observatories, so that visitors can plan their itinerary with an overall view that was previously impossible. The model is complemented by interactive panels that allow visitors to consult information sheets on the most representative species, with photographs, recorded calls and data on their migratory cycles. This is not a static exhibition: each panel invites visitors to touch, press or listen, a design decision intended to capture the attention of the schoolchildren who fill the facilities every school year.

The educational classroom occupies a third of the usable floor space and is equipped with modular tables, a digital whiteboard and optical material for observing samples. Schools in the region now have a resource here that has transformed their visits: they no longer arrive directly at the trail, but instead attend a twenty-minute introductory session in which the basic rules are explained and the ecological value of the space is contextualised. Municipal technicians estimate that this pedagogical filter has notably reduced inappropriate behaviour, such as littering or chasing birds to photograph them. The room is also reserved for scientific bird-ringing workshops, talks by naturalist associations and working meetings for the wetland's own staff.

On the upper floor, the viewpoint offers a one-hundred-and-eighty-degree panorama over the main lagoon and the surrounding reedbed. From this height, the mosaic structure of the wetland is clearly visible: the open waters where waterfowl congregate, the reed beds where rails hide, and the band of tamarisk that separates the protected area from the neighbouring agricultural plots. The viewpoint has two fixed telescopes for free use and interpretive panels that help identify the most common species in each season. Visitors' own binoculars find their best ally here, especially at dawn and dusk, when bird activity reaches its peak.

The audiovisual shown in the main hall summarises the complete history of the wetland in twelve minutes, from its origin as a marshy area to its recent recovery. The images alternate current aerial shots with historical photographs from the 1980s, when the area was an uncontrolled landfill site and the lagoons had been reduced to seasonal puddles. The script avoids a triumphalist tone and focuses on explaining the ecological processes that have allowed the natural recolonisation by fauna. The narration concludes with a sequence of the purple swamphen, one of the site's emblematic species, feeding its chicks among the floating vegetation.

Visitor management has undergone a radical shift since the centre opened. The more than twenty thousand annual visitors received by the Charca de Suárez now pass obligatorily through this entry point, where they are informed of opening hours, behavioural rules and available routes. The visitor services staff, reinforced with new hires, hand out a leaflet with the route map and answer questions about accessibility or trail difficulty. This flow control has made it possible to distribute groups better and avoid overcrowding at the observatories on weekends and holiday periods.

The centre also functions as a gateway for birdwatching tourism, a growing segment along the entire Granada coast. Foreign visitors, mainly British and German, find information here in several languages and the possibility of booking specialised guided tours. The Motril tourist office directs a growing number of travellers to the Charca who are seeking alternatives to sun and beach, especially in spring and autumn, when bird migration turns the wetland into a privileged observation point. Visitor numbers reflect a sustained increase since the inauguration, with peaks of three hundred visitors in a single day during holiday periods.

The investment in this facility is part of the municipal strategy to consolidate the Charca as an educational and tourist benchmark for the region. The building, with its simple lines and materials integrated into the surroundings, has been designed to minimise its visual and energy impact. The green roof reduces the interior temperature in summer, while the large north-facing windows take advantage of natural light without generating reflections that might disturb the birds. Every construction detail responds to a dual requirement: functionality for visitors and absolute respect for the ecosystem that looks in through its windows.
